newsitem.title: UK: BOE comments may tip balance towards UK rate rise.
newsitem.headline: BOE comments may tip balance towards UK rate rise.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George's overnight call for higher interest rates could help tip the balance back towards a possible tightening after the February 5 monetary meeting, economists said.
"I think it's unusually forthright and is going to cause people to revise their recent conclusion that there would be no rate rise in February," said Nigel Richardson of Yamaichi International.
George said sterling's strength should not be used as an excuse to delay a modest pre-emptive tightening in policy.

"There could be real dangers in allowing justified concern about the exchange rate to deflect us for too long from moving gradually to moderate the upswing," the central bank chief said in a speech to bankers in Edinburgh.

This was in marked contrast to Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's comment after the January 15 meeting that the strength of sterling, which reduces imported inflationary pressures, had been a key factor in his decision to leave rates unchanged at 6.0 percent.
"This clearly shows there is no unison between them," Richardson said.
"I think very few people probably imagined they were in total agreement on policy, but this looks to me like a direct and deliberate contradiction of the Chancellor."

Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc, said the Bank was clearly sticking to the view expressed in its November Inflation Report that the strong pound was unlikely to have a major impact on either activity or inflation.

"The Governor is probably firing a broadside at the Chancellor saying that the next Inflaion Report will not contain a major reversal of the bank's view in November," he said. The next Inflation Report will be published in February.

"I would have thought that Clarke would prefer to avoid a major showdown with the Bank of England ahead of the election as the government's handling of the economy will probably feature as a major campaign issue," Shaw said.
But he believes it will take fairly strong fourth quarter GDP figures on January 27 to make Clarke change his mind and agree to raise rates before the election.
Many economists took the view after the January 15 meeting that Clarke might try to "tough it out" and leave rates on hold until the election, which must be held by May 22 at the latest.

An unexpected fall in December manufacturing output and a dip in December RPIX to 3.1 percent from 3.3 percent in November have strengthened the Chancellor's argument that the economy is not beginning to overheat.

However, George said on Monday night that strong growth in money supply and consumer spending could not be sustained for long without jeopardising the government's 2.5 percent for underlying inflation.
"We need to anticipate what is to come and begin to moderate the pace of the upswing before the evidence of imbalance comes through into the statistics," he said.
Sterling briefly touched a 52-month high against the dollar this morning while gilts were a shade easier.
Economists said fresh evidence of a policy rift between Clarke and George could be unsettling for financial markets.
"I think they will probably remain poles apart for the foreseaable future, unless there are developments on the real economy or the prices side which make the chancellor change his mind," Shaw said.
